column4: In the same Queen of Sheba report, this verse says her prior worship besides Allah had held her back; it makes the solar-cult report personal to the ruler and states the barrier that the section associates with being kept from the path.
After the glass-floor scene, the queen says she has wronged herself and submits with Solomon to Allah, Lord of the worlds; this completes the solar-worship report with a specific turn to the Creator.
In another Abrahamic declaration, he disavows what his father and people worship; it repeats the rejection that the section stages through the setting star, moon, and sun.
Abraham excepts the One who created him and says that He will guide him; this joins the section’s Creator and hidaya themes in a parallel Abrahamic formulation.

The verse says God made stars so people can find their way through land and sea darkness; it gives the star from Abraham’s scene a created navigational role, distinct from treating a heavenly light as Lord or from the section’s spiritual guidance.

After mentioning landmarks, the verse says people are guided by the stars (وبالنجم هم يهتدون); the stars that appear in Abraham’s test can guide travel without being objects of worship, while Fatiha asks God for guidance.

This verse identifies the Creator and governor of the heavens and earth and commands worship of Him; its own claim anchors the sun and moon’s calculated courses in 10:5 to the Creator rather than to the luminaries.
The verse praises Allah as creator of the heavens and earth and maker of darkness and light; it concretizes the section’s al-ʿālam dictionary gloss as a created cosmic and luminous order.

Before the kingdom-of-heaven scene and celestial test, Abraham asks his father whether he takes idols as gods and calls his people clearly astray; this is the narrative prelude to the specific star, moon, and sun test in 6:76–78.

After Abraham turns to the Creator in 6:79, this verse says his people dispute with him and he answers that Allah has guided him; its own contribution continues the section’s Abraham-and-guidance scene into the people’s challenge.

Abraham asks how he should fear the partners his people associate with God when they do not fear associating without authority; it continues the same argument after the celestial test and sharpens the rejection of worshiping created things.

The next verse says those who believe without mixing faith with injustice have security and are guided (وهم مهتدون); in Abraham’s argument this answers the section’s fear of becoming among the astray with a stated condition for guidance.

The verse says east and west belong to Allah and wherever people turn is His face (فأينما تولوا فثم وجه الله); it parallels Abraham turning his face to the Creator after seeing heavenly bodies, while its own setting concerns direction of prayer.

The fasting instruction begins with dawn becoming distinguishable and ends the fast at night; it gives a concrete human boundary for the daylight interval that the section defines through the sun’s course.
The cave scene continues by saying the young men are asleep and turned from side to side; it supplies the occupants’ condition after 18:17 describes sunlight shifting away from their cave.

In the same report of a sun-worshiping people, Solomon’s letter begins with بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم, repeating the Fatiha’s opening formula and bringing the section’s Bism and Allah features into the solar-cult passage.

The next line of Solomon’s letter tells the queen not to exalt herself and to come as a submitter; in its political setting this is a concrete response to the people’s sun worship, though the command itself is a ruler’s ultimatum.
Joseph says this scene fulfills his earlier dream; his parents and brothers bow to him, clarifying that the sun and moon bowing in 12:4 are dream symbols for family, not worshiped celestial bodies.

Joseph’s dream shows the sun, moon, and stars prostrating to him, reversing the human prostration to the sun in the Sheba report; 12:100 identifies the scene as a dream fulfilled through his family, so the parallel is symbolic.
